newsitem.title: UK: London gold fixes firmer, palladium hits new high.
newsitem.headline: London gold fixes firmer, palladium hits new high.

text.p: Precious metal markets were mostly firmer on Tuesday after all except palladium came under selling pressure overnight, traders said.
Palladium was pushed up to a fresh recent high fixing at $177.50 per ounce, having escaped the selling which mainly stemmed from New York but followed through into Tokyo.
It was its highest fix since April 5,1995. "It's to do with (Russian) non-delivery, Tokyo positions and fund interest all happening together," a dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $342.50 per ounce, up from $340.70 on Monday and after a 40 yen per gram daily limit fall in Japan.
The weakness in Tokyo came on long liquidation after a rising yen pushed the dollar below 112 yen.
"You would expect a move to pick it up from bargain buying. The funds and producers sold it on Monday," a dealer said.
However he added, "this is not a northbound market" echoing technical analysts' views that gold would struggle to get beyond $345.00.

Sentiment in gold turned from bearish to depressed late last week when Germany announced it planned to revalue its modestly priced gold reserves closer to market values in order to help it achieve European Monetary Union convergence criteria.
The market view was that this made gold into just another asset and could encourage other central banks to mobilise their reserves for budgetary purposes.
Karen Jones of Credit Suisse First Boston said gold should find good underlying support between $340.00 and $338.00, while she was pegging $345 as a stiff upside barrier.
"Gold is due for a bounce, though any upside gains will be limited," Jones commented.
Action might also be constrained today by the U.S. monetary policy advisory FOMC meeting later.
The New York June palladium contract closed up $5.90 at $178.00 and buying in Tokyo and later London lifted spot.
Lease rates for a month were quoted at 25-26 percent, exacerbated by short positions in Tokyo and the absence of Russian deliveries, dealers said.
They were less precise about platinum's $391.50/$392.50 quotation, up $2.25. "Unless you need it for liquidity, there is no point in buying. People just wait and see," one said.
The premium over gold at almost $50.00 meant platinum was too expensive to encourage platinum-gold spread plays, he added.
Silver also rallied reaching $4.72/$4.74, up six cents.
